en: I, Shifan, bow my head in greeting to the Elder Abbot of Lingyan.
It has been a long time since our last parting; during that interval, I received your letter, but thereafter I had no knowledge of your movements or whereabouts.

At the end of the year, I suddenly received this letter and its accompanying missive while aboard a boat in Suzhou, and thus learned of your ordination as an abbot, an event made public by the various monastic communities.
I am deeply comforted by these words from your venerable heart. Since you have been appointed as the abbot, you differ from ordinary monks;
you now hold the office of abbot, for which there have long been established rules and precedents. You must follow and implement each one of them. Most essential is this:
to extensively gather those who come to study through the fundamental matter of the Way, while also providing for them according to your own capacity and removing their excesses.

The peril of failing to reach [the goal] will, over time, naturally manifest as a karmic retribution. You, who value the long-standing traditions of the monastic groves (*saṃghārāma*), have witnessed the corruptions of the present age;
you should examine this in silence and ensure that you do not lose your footing and fall into their ranks, becoming an object of ridicule for those with true discernment.
I am old; I have resided at Mount Wufeng for seventeen years now. Following the gradual process after my petition was granted, I sought a plan for seclusion. Only...
There will be time for this sooner or later. I have sent you a set of Dharma robes, one size too large, which you may wear once upon ascending the hall.
As for the illusory body that has no pre-existing form, I shall entrust that to another day. I offer this brief reply while on the road; it is not very detailed.
Regarding all else, you should cherish yourself for the sake of the Great Vehicle (Zongmen). Sincerely yours.
The Reverend Shifan bows his head and respectfully presents the table of contents for the Recorded Sayings of the Venerable Elder Wuan, Abbot of Lingyan.

Recorded by Attendant Jingyun. Compiled as the Three Gates:
the Gate of Delusion and Enlightenment, and the Two Paths of the Sage and the Ordinary. With his hand, he makes a single stroke and says: "In total, I grant [this] to all..."
People have opened it up; let us all be summoned to enter into realization at once.
In the Buddha Hall, there is one Śākyamuni and two Pratyekabuddhas—how truly marvelous! Even so, it is thus.
[The Master] burns incense and prostrates within the Way of Benevolence and Righteousness.
Taking his place at the abbot’s seat, he holds his staff horizontally across his body and says, "Is there anyone who disregards peril and ruin? After a long pause, he says, "As expected."
The note states: "From the very beginning, everyone has been gripped by this 'something' and held fast; there is no place to turn or breathe.
Master Ning usually nods his head crosswise with a single flavor, yet when he arrives here, even all the skillful means of his entire life cannot free him from it.
Tell me, why is it so? Public justice has already been served."

Pointing to the Dharma seat, he sat upon it, severing all distinctions. Radiant and majestic in the presence of all, even the Lamp-King of Mount Sumeru would have to look up at the sky and rub his forehead in awe.

Ascending the seat, he offered prayers for the Emperor, followed by prayers for the local prefectures and counties. Then he said: "This single offering of incense was born without the aggregates of form."
A land of Yang. It emerges from a realm beyond thought and deliberation. The softest among the stubborn, the harshest among the fierce.

If one happens to catch its scent even once for no particular reason, it immediately causes one to lose everything of their entire life. Today, before this assembly of devas and humans, I shall burn it in the open light.
This is offered for the sake of the Great Master, the currently residing Abbot of Mount Jing, Chan Master Fojian Yuanzhao, to repay the milk of the Dharma.
He took his seat. (The questions and answers are not recorded. He then said: "If Śākyamuni had not appeared in this world, he would have preached for forty-nine years;
if the Patriarch had not come from the West, Shaolin would possess the wondrous secret. Therefore it is said: 'The Dharma has no coming or going; it has no characteristic of movement or change.'"
Yesterday morning it was Nulusi; today it is Lingyan. There has never been a trace of movement or shifting; how could there be any trace of coming or going?
If this is so, then the eyes of the Buddhas and Patriarchs of the past, and the nostrils of all the monks in the world—[the Master] suddenly picks up his staff and strikes once, saying:
"All have been pierced at once by my staff. Throughout the entire universe and the great earth, furthermore—"
There is not even a hair’s breadth of leakage. Nevertheless, tell me: where does this merit reside? Leaning on his staff, he said:
"When the waves of the four seas are stilled, the dragon sleeps soundly; when the clouds of the nine heavens are clear, the crane flies high."
Again, he cites the paths of the three sages: "When I meet people, I come forth; having come forth, I do not act for the sake of others"—this is the path of Xinghua.

"When I meet people, I do not come forth; having come forth, I immediately act for the sake of others"—this is [the path of] the other. He comments: Of these two great elders, one went ahead but did not arrive.
One person at the end was excessive. Examining it from beginning to end, they were entirely lacking one essential point.
Layman Ning stayed in mountain caves and lived in seclusion until his time had passed; for no reason, he was pushed out by others to perform such actions.
Now that he has come forth, tell me: does he act as a man or not? He then said: "With a free hand, I carve square and round; naturally, it accords with the rules."
That evening’s informal discourse: The Tathāgata has but one teaching and no second; the Patriarchs have but the Mind-transmission and no other transmission. Thus it is said:
"The hook is cast across the four seas, yet it catches only the fierce dragon; the mysterious mechanism beyond the norm is for seeking those who understand.
Nevertheless, as for the single phrase according to the command—how is it? "The north wind sweeps the earth and the hundred grasses die; the lotus flowers bloom."
"Late Cold in the Growth of Peanuts. [The Master] again cited Deshan’s small-scale public address (*xiao-can*), which said: "Tonight, I will not answer questions.
At that time, a monk stepped forward, and Deshan immediately struck him. The monk said, "I have not even asked a question; why do you strike me?"
Shan said, "Where are you from? The monk replied, "I am a man from Silla. Shan said, "Before you have even stepped onto the ship's railing, thirty blows of the staff are in order for you!
[The Master] comments: Old man Deshan can let go but cannot gather in; he can kill but cannot bring to life.
Had he wished to fully carry out his command at that time, he ought to have struck him with the staff and driven him out immediately.
The Dharma robe arrived from Mount Jing. The Master held up the robe, called to the assembly, and said:
"At the head of Dayu Ridge, it could not be lifted; why then is it now in Lingyan’s hands? Do you all know the essential point?
If you do, then you will know that from the very beginning, Buddha to Buddha the hand has been passed on, and patriarch to patriarch the transmission has continued—precisely and without partiality."
"Continuously there is a standard. Should one not yet know it, [the master] then holds up the dharma robe and says:
'This was personally handed down by the Elder Yuanzhao of Mount Jing. (He then puts it on.)"
Ascending the hall, he called to the assembly, saying: "Donning the skin of a jackal, one lets out the roar of a lion; pointing east as west, taking non-existence for existence.
Startling the Dharmakāya into hiding within the Big Dipper! He let out a shout and descended from his seat.
Ascending the Hall for the commencement of the retreat: "The Tathāgatas of the past have already perfected this gate—wrong!
The Bodhisattvas of the present are each likewise perfectly luminous—wrong! Those who practice and study in the future should train in this very way—wrong!
Do you all know these three points where they go astray? If you can understand them, it will not hinder you from sharing in this summer retreat; otherwise, it may.
Nevertheless, listen as I point out a single error from the very beginning, thereby opening the eyes of the Buddhas and Patriarchs of the past and twisting the nostrils of all monks in the world.
Tell me, what about another error? [He suddenly picks up his staff and] says:
"Staff! Do you not have anything to say? Come forth and, taking error for error, speak! [He strikes once with the staff.]”
He said, "Rancid rice and a mud tea stove.
Entering the hall, he said, "The teachings state: 'Depart from the mark of verbal expression; depart from the mark of written characters; depart from the mark of mental conditioning.
Ultimately equal, there is no change or alteration. He suddenly called out to the assembly, "Regarding such talk, how could a shrimp ever leap out of its shell?"
Even if you obtain the measure, if you approach the gate of the patch-robed monk, you are still separated by heavy barriers. What, after all, is the matter?
The lotus leaf is round and round, as round as a mirror; the water chestnut horn is sharp and sharp, as sharp as an awl. The wind blows and the tufted cotton ball rolls away;
the rain beats upon the pear blossoms and the butterflies fly.
Zhongxia ascended the hall and said: "In this summer retreat of ninety days, half has already passed unnoticed.
Tending the ox-calf, take care not to let it follow after external objects. Grip the nose-rope tightly; do not allow it to become slack. Thus, throughout the twelve periods of the day."
From time to time, without interruption, he attained mastery. Even when challenged, he would not depart; he accepted the words of others without wavering or changing.
Facing the situation directly, responding to the occasion directly—how is it, ultimately? After a long silence, he said: "Do not move."
As soon as one moves, horns sprout. Small Precept-Lifting *Sīmā* Assembly *Xichan*:
There is no dharma before the eyes; the intent lies right before the eyes. Ten thousand miles east and west, eight thousand miles south and north.
For this reason, Bodhidharma did not come to the Eastern Land, and the Second Patriarch did not go to the Western Heaven. Examining this from the outset, one sees only one side.

Even if one were to go east or west, heading directly toward a place ten thousand miles away where there is not an inch of grass, it would be much like pushing a cart through mud or sailing a boat on dry land.
Even if you all say that as soon as one leaves the gate there is grass, though this may be so for a gentleman—
"Though we share the same wind across a thousand miles, one cannot avoid seeing smoke from behind a mountain. How can this compare to simply following the flow with ease—following the flow with ease?
When hungry, eat; when thirsty, drink; when walking, sit; when weary, sleep. Thus, naturally, every place flows toward the source, and at every turn, the tracks coincide.
Transverse and longitudinal, one attains the wondrous; the eight openings and seven holes are all there. Yet, if you do not accept even this, then how is it? He struck his knee once and said:
Unaware that day turns to night, how can one teach people to remain young? Again, a monk asked Yunmen:
"At the end of autumn and the beginning of summer, whether going east or west, if someone on the road ahead asks you something, how will you answer?
Yunmen said: "The assembly, step back! The monk asked: "Where is my fault? Yunmen said: "Give me back the money for ninety days' worth of meals."
[The monk] comes forward. The Master picks up the case and says: "This old fellow Yunmen, by hesitating when he should have acted decisively, instead invited further confusion.

At that moment, as soon as [the monk] asked the question, he should have struck him across the back. Then, waiting for him to say, 'Where did my fault lie? he could have said, 'When meeting people, do not speak erroneously.'"

When Daogu arrived at the hall for the formal lecture, he called to the assembly, saying: "The stringless lute—its pointing and its intent are profound. Such a novel and refined melody must encounter a true connoisseur.
Now that a connoisseur has been found, let us try playing a single movement. He then held his staff horizontally and made the gesture of strumming a lute, asking:
"Do you understand? The infinite meaning of the high mountains and flowing waters; the vast expanse of a thousand-foot precipice."

Ascending the hall, he addressed the assembly, saying: "On the festivals of Cold Food and Pure Brightness, when every household performs the rites of ancestral worship, the wooden man sighs in vain and the stone woman sheds twin tears.
Only the practitioner beneath the forest trees has severed study and dwells in non-action;
knowing nothing and understanding nothing at all, he takes up the unperforated flute of Shaolin and blows it against the wind, then blows it with the wind. Good brother!"

Ascending the hall for the commencement of the summer retreat (*jiezhi*). In various quarters, there is the summer retreat and the commencement of the *kṣetra* (monastic discipline); at Lingyan, there is likewise the commencement of the summer retreat.
Although these follow the same general regulations, within them there are great differences. How so? Zhaozhou hangs a gourd from the eastern wall.
Ascending the hall on the Double Fifth Festival, he held up his staff and addressed the assembly, saying: "This staff has no partiality; it has never been hidden throughout the entire realm.
It is entirely without form or shadow. He struck once to the left and said: "All monsters and spirits are utterly eradicated.
He struck once to the right and said: "Buddhas and demons are both swept away. "After they have been swept away, what then? He threw down the staff and said: "Throughout the heavens..."
The Imperial Way is without obstruction.
Upon receiving the news of the passing of my late teacher, Yuanzhao of Mount Jing, I ascended the hall and addressed the assembly, saying:
"Stubbornness is not simply being stubbornly soft; it is uniquely capable of attempting to propel a boat upon dry land. Suddenly propelling it toward the Dragon Gate, its traces are no longer known."
"Go over there! How many have their hopes severed, left empty and despondent? Again, they sigh and lament with tears streaming down. [He strikes the meditation seat once and says:
"How can one obtain phoenix-glue to mend the broken strings? [He raises his voice in mourning and addresses the assembly:
"I have a single phrase. It is neither sealed nor established; it does not reside at the tip of the tongue, nor is it a place of thought or recollection. If you people..."
You must know how to attain intimacy. The Elder Yuanzhao of Jingshan is right now, upon the eyelashes of all of you, emitting a great radiance and preaching freely with his mouth.
You must listen with urgent attention. If this is not yet so, you will be weeping for the blue sky amidst the blue sky.

Ascending the hall to express his response to the prayer for rain, he held up his staff and showed it to the assembly, saying: "This staff transforms into a dragon, grasping the clouds and swirling the mist;
its wondrous response is unfathomable. It pours down a great deluge, so that the four seas are all interconnected. The five grains ripen, and all things attribute their success to it.
With bellies drummed and songs sung, people forget the affairs of the world. He struck a circle with the staff and said: "The sun remains as it was before."
At the eastern gate of the sea, he threw down his staff and descended from the seat to give the *xiaoxian* (summer retreat) *xican* (private instruction).
"Directly beneath, it is still difficult to comprehend; seeking through words only makes it more remote.

If one speaks of Buddhas and Patriarchs, they are abruptly separated by the ends of the earth. To simply accept it as such is already unfit for debate; how much less so for one who has ended their summer retreat?"
"Let it be! To take a wax figure as proof—how utterly deplorable! Lingyan makes such an announcement; has anyone here experienced a sudden, profound realization?
He strikes the meditation seat once and says: "Unprovoked, the wild goose came last night, startling autumn from the rear pond. He then raises another case.
Baling addressed the assembly, saying: "It is not the wind moving; it is not the banner moving. Since it is neither wind nor banner, where do you place it?
If there is anyone who can act as the patriarch’s advocate, come forth and meet Baling.
Later, Xuedou said: "It is the wind moving; it is the banner moving. Since it is both wind and banner, where do you place it? If there is anyone who can act as Baling’s advocate...
He acted as the presiding master and came forth to meet Xuedou. The Master [Zhaozhou] took up the case, saying:

"Everyone says these two ancient worthies struck and praised one another, their golden sounds and jade resonances illuminating the past and soaring through the present. Little do they realize that one was far too frugal and the other was far too extravagant."
There was a man who acted as host for two venerable elders; he came forth to meet Lingyan.

When the hall was opened to thank those who had undertaken the construction, [Lingyan said]: "Tearing down the fence on the east to patch the wall on the west; building a framework upon the void; using one wedge to drive out another.
In time, it will soar over the ravines and tower above the clouds—truly, you must know that no extra effort is required. Such words are truly excellent.
[The Master] laughed. "Why? Just as one has finished rolling the pellets, one must immediately mold the Vajra.
He descended from his seat and ascended the hall. He raised the following case: A monk asked Baling, "Are the meaning of the Patriarchs and the meaning of the Teachings the same or different?

Baling said, "When the rooster is cold, it climbs the tree; when the duck is cold, it enters the water. Master Yuanzhao said, "The monks of Sichuan are coarse; the monks of Zhejiang are elegant. The Master [continued]: "..."
The Master picks up the case and says: "Although these two elders each excel in their own family style, it cannot be denied that their levels of excellence are unequal.
Lingyan also has a way of speaking. If someone asks whether the meaning of the Patriarchs and the meaning of the Teachings are the same or different, he simply says: 'The hawk soars to the heavens.'"
"Fish leap in the deep pool.
He ascended the hall, held up his staff, and showed it to the assembly, saying: "Yesterday, when I entered the town for the conclusion of the ritual, I unintentionally acquired an object.
It is neither long nor short, neither square nor round; it is neither blue, yellow, red, nor white. Though humble, its value is as great as Saha World."
"Venerable Sir! It is so precious that not even a single character could be purchased for it. I did not dare keep it hidden away.

Now that I have returned today, I cannot avoid beating the drum and ascending the hall to distribute it equally among you all. He taps the table once and says, "One plus three; two plus six. He throws down [the staff] and says, "Collect!"
The Master ascends the hall for the occasion of bathing the Buddha. He cites the case of Yaoshan, who, while Zun the monk, the temple director, was in the midst of bathing the Buddha, asked him:
"You can bathe only this one; can you also bathe that one? Zun replied, "Bring me that one first.
Yaoshan then desisted. The Master comments: "As soon as the old fellow Yaoshan opened his foul mouth, his local dialect was revealed, leading [Zun] astray."
Punna followed the heterodox and pursued evil. At that time, had he been expected to speak thus, one need only have ladled out fragrant water to bathe the Buddha;
it would have guaranteed that Yaoshan’s mouth could not close once opened. Lingyan does not ask about this or that;
today happens to be the eighth day of the fourth month. I dare guarantee that you all have not even dreamed of this mountain monk’s fine body hair.
Record of the Sayings from Nanchan Fusheng Temple in Wuxi, Changzhou;
compiled by Attendant Qingze.
Pointing to the Main Gate: "The style of our gate stands alone and precarious; if you are a true descendant of Linji, then please enter directly."
The blade enters straight through. He lets out a shout.
"The Buddha Hall—Śākyamuni and Maitreya are his slaves. Who is he? Inserting incense, he says: "Just look when the four corners tread upon the ground."
The Great Sage’s Hall appeared in Yangzhou; he left his staff here, and the precious stupa towers high into the void.
Its fame and radiance stir ten thousand li away; it benefits all things by responding to myriad capacities, like the moon dividing its reflection across many waters.
I have come to burn a single incense offering, gazing upon it once and prostrating once. Let people say that I fall down only to rise up again.
Taking his place at the abbot’s seat, he held his staff horizontally across his lap and called out to the assembly, “I, this mountain monk, sit here waiting for you to grasp it.
After a long silence, he said, “Do you all feel the heaviness upon the crown of your heads? He then cast down the staff and rose.
[The Master] held up the official dispatch. "This is from the Palace Secretary of the Department of Transportation, who orchestrates the workings of creation and holds the pivot of heaven and earth.

From within a state of non-mind, he has brought this forth in the open, so that those who have not yet believed may believe, and those who have not yet heard may hear. This mountain monk receives it with the highest reverence;
who would not submit to his instructions?"
Pointing to the Dharma seat, he said: "The upward path is slippery; standing like a cliff ten thousand fathoms high, it is perilous.
Southern Chan does not establish stages or steps; it cuts off head-on and sits directly upon it.
[He offered incense for] the Emperor, followed by incense for the Prefectures and Counties. Taking his seat, he sat. (Question and answer not recorded. Then he said: "The intent of Vulture Peak—"
The true mechanism of Shaoshi stands solitary and towering, giving rise to a whistling wind; it directly transcends emotion and leaves behind views, surpassing form and mounting sound.
Gathering and releasing at will, there is nothing that cannot be done. Thus, when dwelling by the seashore, one constantly hears the ebb and flow of the tide, its roar vast and surging;
when staying by Liangxi Creek, one merely sees the boats loading and unloading, their comings and goings bustling and incessant.
Host and guest meet; wind and clouds converge. At such a moment as this, how can one transmit the message?
After a long silence, he said: "The seventy-two peaks of Lake Dongting are green. [He] then cited the story of Master Niaoke.
When Minister Bai asked him, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? Niaoke replied, "Commit no evil; practice all that is good. The Minister said, "Even a three-year-old child..."
"The child also understands how to speak thus. Niaokuo said, "Though a three-year-old child can speak it, an eighty-year-old old man cannot practice it.
The Master (Zhaozhou) commented: "The Minister holds the sun and moon of Confucius in his hands and wears the golden seal of Vairocana at his waist;
he casually conveys this message, far transcending the common run. Although Niaokuo was direct and immediate in his response, alas—"
Easy to see, yet difficult to clarify. Do you all know where the ancient masters acted for the sake of others? They split apart Mount Hua, revealing its celestial beauty;
they released the Yellow River, letting its current flow clear.
That evening’s informal discourse: A broken-legged cauldron, a cracked wooden ladle—handleless and without a master, difficult to grasp or fathom.
Held crosswise or used upside down, breaking two into three; pressed straight or lifted sideways, pierced through in seven ways and eight holes.

Since the secret transmission at Vulture Peak and the single-lineage transmission at Shaoshi, this has been unmistakably selfless and consistently authoritative. If one observes it with the true eye, how profound it is!
"The household is secluded, yet the utensils are broken. Nevertheless, who clearly understands this intent? Together we shall uphold the ancient family style. Again, he cites Master Bāzāo.
A monk asked, "Without falling into any conditions, I ask the Master to point directly. Bāzāo said, "There is a question; there is an answer. [The Master] comments:
"Bāzāo’s reception of beings and response to their capacities was quite adept at leveling the high and conforming to the low. Examine this closely."
In the future, one cannot avoid being mired in the mud and water. If you ask about Nanquan, he did not fall into any conditions; I beg the Master to point directly.
[The Master] picks up his staff and strikes. If you feel even the slightest sensation of pain, you shall certainly not fail him or betray his kindness.

New Year’s Eve Small Sermon: “The mind turns with the myriad objects; where it turns, it can indeed be profound. If one recognizes one’s nature while following the flow, there is neither joy nor sorrow.
This mountain monk is like a government official, not free to act as he pleases; he must simply follow the current and flow with it.

Thus, having newly arrived, I am yet unaware of the bustle at the well and hearth; I have had no leisure to change my voice or alter my tune in bidding farewell to the old year and welcoming the new. [Kitchen...]
There is not even a speck of flour for flies to swarm over; there is not even a thread to tie a sack for ants. Internally empty, externally empty, internally and externally empty.

Much anxiety, much deliberation, much affliction. The year has ended and the month has passed. The destitute sigh in exhaustion; the hungry clamor in hunger. The pillar in the courtyard frowns in the dark;
the lantern laughs with clapping hands. But tell me, what is it that he laughs at? After a long silence, he said: "Vipaśyin Buddha."
"Apply your mind early; even until now, you have not attained the subtlety. [The Master] cited Yunmen’s address to the assembly:

"Regarding the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the teachings, and the coming of Bodhidharma from the West—if one lets these pass by, that is unacceptable. If one does not let them pass, they do not even merit a single shout."
Xuedou uttered a shout and then said, "A fine drink! If you, the assembly, wish for your nostrils to reach the heavens, discern this one shout.
The Master [Zhaozhou] commented: "It is not that the two ancient worthies lacked the ability to sing a high note, but when one examines their actions closely,"
Amidst a great clamor and commotion, he ascended the hall and recited the verse on Lingyun’s awakening upon seeing peach blossoms: "For thirty years I have sought the sword-wielder;
(Commentary: A fool wandering outside. How many times have the leaves fallen and the branches sprouted? (Having endured the bitterness of frost and snow. Since then...
Once you have seen the peach blossoms (calling a bell a jar), even until now you shall have no further doubts (a fox testing the water).
Even if there were one who attained self-awakening without a teacher, they would not be fit to wash the feet of Nan Chan. As for Xuan Sha’s words: "How perfectly true! How perfectly true!
I dare guarantee that you, elder brother, have not yet reached the ultimate. What about this? After a long silence, he said: "I was once..."
The profligate especially pities the traveler; out of love for the cup, he spares the one who grows drunk.
On the third day of the third month, the Great Sage’s birthday, he ascends the hall and cites National Teacher Sishou Dashi.
Formerly, someone asked him: "In which country do you reside? He replied: "Which country? (A comment: His teeth are like iron pegs. Again, he was asked:
"What is his surname? He replied, "His surname is He" (the tip of his tongue touching the upper palate). [The Master] remarked: "Surging eastward and sinking westward;
sevenfold and eightfold in its movements—there is no lack of great sages indeed, yet alas, all their ugliness is laid bare. On this occasion of his birthday, he took up his staff and said:
The staff cannot help but provide a commentary appropriate to the time and season. He strikes it once and says: "On a late day, the rivers and mountains are beautiful;
in the spring breeze, the flowers and grasses are fragrant. The mud is soft and the swallows fly; on the warm sands, the mandarin ducks sleep. He then hurls down the staff.
When Master Yǎnxī Fózhi of Jìngshān ascended the hall, he said: "The waters of East Gully are clear and limpid; their source is distant and their flow long.
The waves surge and boil. Entering from this point, one does not know how many times it has been done.
This may be so, but as for National Preceptor Cānshī, when he passed by Liángxī, he suddenly gave a squeeze to the nostrils of the Great Sage of Sīzhōu, until there was nowhere left to go."

He let out a breath. Was this to suppress the worthy and degrade them to the lowly? Or was it a display of spiritual powers (*ṛddhi-vikrīḍita*)? After a long while, he said: "A gentleman may be eight [feet tall].

When Duanqiao of Jingci went up to the hall for the formal lecture, he cited the passage where Ānanda asked Kāśyapa: "Aside from the transmission of the golden robe, what else did the World-Honored One transmit to you?"
Regarding the "What is this? koan from the *Biézhuan*: The Master’s verse says: "The younger brother responds when the elder brother calls; He brings his own family's disgrace to light.
He knocks over the bannerpole; The entire mechanism leaks through. Though the moon over West Lake may shine like day, How can it compare to Nanzen’s iron broom?"

Tiantong Zhibieshan ascended the hall for the *shangtang* ceremony. He raised the example of Furong visiting Master Shixing’s *shangtang*, where [Furong] took the staff in his right hand, placed it on his left side, and said:
"Were it not for my elder brother Furong, it would have been difficult to fully comprehend."

He then descended from his seat. The Master commented: "In the functioning of true nature, although one may move to the left or to the right, alas, it inevitably results in doing something out of place.
Nan Chan also wished to emulate the works of the ancients; he could not help but turn poverty into wealth and prepare the ritual with 'hemp-soup' (a metaphor for a hollow or forced performance)."
He threw down his staff and said, "Were it not for my elder brother, Tiantong, it would be difficult to fully comprehend this. He then descended from the seat.
In the small assembly for the commencement of the retreat, he said: "The golden crow hurries and the jade hare speeds;
a hundred years of time passes in a single instant. Suddenly grasping the staff, he said: "Only this staff—hard and rugged, black and weathered; unchanging and faceless. Three.
The moon protects life; for ninety days, one restrains the feet. By means of this, one may attain the twelve hours such that one is not hurried by those twelve hours.

He further applied the "winter melon seal": "I possess the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye and the wondrous mind of Nirvāṇa;
I entrust them to Mahākāśyapa. Upon a heap of dust, he added more dust. At that time, from among the assembly of a million people, there was suddenly a man who—
If one turns over the surface skin, one will see that there are many deficiencies and omissions.

After Gautama entered nirvana, Mahākāśyapa, Ānanda, and the other great disciples compiled the teachings he had spoken during the preceding forty-nine years, arranging them into the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the canon.
How could these have merely filled the dragon palaces or overflowed the oceanic treasuries? As for those who are free from attachment...

The Bodhisattvas Vasubandhu, Dharmapāla, Aśvaghoṣa, and others, deeply concerned that those of inferior faculties and limited wisdom would find it difficult to comprehend the Buddha’s principles, each composed treatises to provide explanations.
These were designated as the Tripiṭaka—the Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma collections—and were gradually transmitted to the land of Tang, though they remained incomplete.
Consequently, masters such as Xuanzang traveled personally to India to request the Sūtras, Vinayas, and Śāstras.

Returning to the Eastern Land, he saw that all people were truly difficult to enlighten and lead to understanding. He consequently composed commentaries and sub-commentaries to explain [the teachings], so as to make them easy for all people to understand.
As these accumulated over time, they piled up like mountains. From that time forth...
Those who study the commentaries and sub-commentaries on the Sutras, Vinaya, and Shastras take them to be the study of mere words and consider this to be the ultimate study.
They do not believe that the principle of the "separate transmission outside the teachings" is the ultimate Way; this is truly pitiable.
Yet they do not realize that for those who cling to the literal text, apart from black ink and white paper, how can they proceed? Often, when [the teacher] speaks of gold...

It is like a jade tucked in the mouth; it is difficult to explain or share with others. When the thirtieth day of the twelfth month arrives and the moment of birth-and-death comes upon you, the path ahead will be vast and desolate, and you will not know where you are going.
Only then will you realize that the study of words and letters truly yields no power. By then, what regret can avail?
After Kāśyapa, Ānanda, and the others had compiled the Dharma-treasury, they no longer set eyes upon it; they simply took up the spiritual...
Mount Shishuang secretly transmitted the essential teaching of not relying on words and letters to point directly to the human mind. This has been passed down from patriarch to patriarch.
Therefore, Ānanda asked Kāśyapa, "Elder brother, besides the golden robe, what else did the World-Honored One transmit?
Kāśyapa called out, "Ānanda! Ānanda responded. Kāśyapa said, "Throw down the banner-pole in front of the gate. This very thing—
This is the "winter melon seal" obtained by those who came before, handed down in succession until it reached the twenty-eighth patriarch, the Grand Master Bodhidharma.
After he attained the Dharma and shattered the six schools, he received a prophetic mandate and traveled ten thousand *li* across the ocean.
He journeyed through Liang and Wei, teaching solely the essential method of pointing directly to the human mind without relying on written words at Shaolin.
For nine years he faced a wall. There, Shen Guang appeared before him seeking the Way.

This Shen Guang was one who had mastered the teachings of Confucianism, as well as the various schools and hundred masters of thought, penetrating both ancient and modern times, such that there was nothing he did not understand. He was also thoroughly versed in the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the Buddhist scriptures.
There was nothing he did not master thoroughly. He questioned the Patriarch Bodhidharma, saying, "May I hear of the unsurpassed, wondrous Way of all Buddhas?
The Patriarch Bodhidharma replied, "How could the unsurpassed, wondrous Way of all Buddhas be attained by one of inferior roots, small wisdom, and lowly disposition?
Thereupon, Shen Guang severed his arm before him and stood in the snow until it reached his waist. The Patriarch then asked:
Huineng asked, "By what means do you seek it? Shenkang replied, "My mind is not at peace; I beg the Master to bring peace to my mind.

The Patriarch answered, "Bring forth your mind, and I shall pacify it for you. Shenkang searched exhaustively through the various schools of Confucianism, the hundred masters of the secular arts, and the three vehicles and twelve divisions of the Buddhist teachings, yet he found not a single word that corresponded.
He then responded with absolute sincerity, saying, "I have sought my mind within and without, but I cannot find it."
It cannot be grasped. It is like chasing a dog until it is pressed against a wall;

when one’s calculations are exhausted and one’s strength spent, the Patriarch simply lightly places the "pumpkin seal" upon the gateway of the face and says, "I have finished settling your mind for you. Now tell me:
how does this differ from, and how is it distinct from, the World-Honored One’s response to Subhūti regarding the principle of "abiding thus and subduing the mind thus"? Try to test this.
Upon seeing this, Shen Guang received this seal of approval (*inka*). Taking up the master’s lineage, he became the Second Patriarch, who in turn succeeded to the Third Patriarch.

This latter was a layman in white robes who was thoroughly proficient in both Confucian and Buddhist teachings. Suddenly afflicted by a wind-related ailment, he came specifically to seek the Dharma from the Second Patriarch, saying:
"I, your disciple, am bound by a wind ailment; I beg the Master to repent for my transgressions. The Second Patriarch did not change his posture at all.
The First Patriarch said, "Bring forth your offense so that I may repent it for you. The Third Patriarch did likewise;

when he had thoroughly investigated and found no means [of locating it], he said, "I have searched for the offense both internally and externally, but it is utterly unobtainable. The Second Patriarch then took this very seal of realization.
Yituo said: "I have finished confessing your transgressions for you. From Buddha to Buddha, hands were extended; from Patriarch to Patriarch, they were transmitted until this very day.
Therefore, the episode of the Flower held aloft at Vulture Peak is called 'a separate practice outside the teachings.
Since it is already included within the Sūtras, Vinayas, and Śāstras, it is not recorded as a standalone item. Thus one should know that this school of ours is like a vast ocean."

The hundred rivers flow in different directions, yet all return to the same single taste. Just as the great void encompasses all worlds throughout ten billion Ganges-sands without exception, so it is said:
before the world existed, this nature already existed; when the world perishes, this nature does not perish.
Before the Buddhas appeared in the world and before the Patriarchs came from the West, the constant radiance was ever-present within every person.

Previously, each and every one stood like a cliff rising ten thousand fathoms; in sages it did not increase by so much as a hair’s breadth, and in ordinary people it did not decrease by so much as a hair’s breadth.
It was only because of the difference between delusion and awakening that there arose the distinction between the sacred and the profane.

Consequently, those who cling to the study of literal texts became numerous; thus, the inherent nature could not be manifested. They turned their backs on awakening and conformed to the dust of the senses, abandoning the root to pursue the branches. This is because—
It is for this reason that Confucianism also says: "The gentleman applies himself to the root. When the root is established, the Way arises.
This root is precisely one's own natal destiny (*ming ben-yuan chen*) and original countenance (*benlai mianmu*). Only when this root is established can the Way arise;
if the root is not established, by what means could the Way arise? This is the superficial teaching of the Confucians, yet even they are able to say this much.
If it is this intimate [instruction], how much more so the wondrous essence that is not transmitted?

You people here, if you truly wish to practice Chan and study the Way, to investigate and clarify the great matter of birth and death, and to take thorough realization as your goal, first you must possess a firm and enduring body and mind.
You must first set aside all that you have previously studied—the various schools of philosophy, the hundred families of learning, and the four-six style of prose.

Study of the sutras, vinaya, and śāstras, the learning of written characters, as well as seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing—all such evil knowledge and evil perceptions, all these various poisons—must be cast away to other worlds.
Only then may you step back and attend to yourself, letting go of teachings so that they do not merely result in empty toil.
Simply take a single phrase from the ancients and paste it upon the tip of your nose. Day and night, three times each, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down;

in every movement, turn, bow, or gesture—diligently and earnestly, with a resolve that defies death and surrenders life—engage with it until you are worn out by it, without the slightest interruption.
Have you not heard it said: "To be absent for even a moment is to be like a dead man"? Thus, continue to bring it forth and examine it, day after day.
After many years, when the conditions have fully ripened, suddenly there is a "spat" and a break, a "crack" and a severance. Having undergone a great death once, one's own eye opens wide;
the natural radiance of the original ground suddenly manifests before one. Only then does one know that it was originally only within oneself.
It does not lie with others; it lies simply in not doubting the Buddha, not doubting the Patriarchs, and not doubting the tongues of the old monks of the world.
Therefore it is said: "To practice Chan, one must attain awakening; having awakened, one must meet a person.

If you do not seek certification from an enlightened master, it is like a student who has passed the examinations and attained the highest degree, yet fails to receive a promotion in rank—it is merely that.
In vain. Once you have obtained the handle and gained mastery, you will know from where birth comes and to where death goes;
regarding the coming and going of birth and death, there will not be the slightest doubt. When you reach such a state, it is only then called the great rest and the great cessation.
There is no birth-and-death to fear, and no Bodhi to seek. Throughout the entire world of the ten directions, from top to bottom, this is the Reality.

Regarding the reality of the human body, have you not seen what the ancient masters said? "If there is one person who awakens to the truth and returns to the source, the empty space of the ten directions will all vanish away.
This is surely not false. Thereafter, with the fragrance of the Way ripening into fruit, they enter the entanglements and extend their hands, responding to capacities and connecting with beings;
naturally, they possess ample leisure and ease. If, however, you are half-believing and half-doubting, then today you ask.
One phrase today; tomorrow, ask about another phrase. Rest for several more days, and then look again at the manual until you remember two phrases. Ask about them, "How is it? What is it?
with a steady and composed manner. Furthermore, there is a class of people of meager merit and icchantikas who are solely intent on scrutinizing others while failing to scrutinize themselves;
they are certainly unfit to serve as the grass for the seed, and one must distance oneself from such as these.
Such a person would not have even dreamed of reaching it by the year of the donkey.
Have you not seen how Master Liang-sui could lecture with profound depth and mastery, yet realized that the study of scriptural doctrines and literary texts is not the ultimate?
Hearing that the gate of Zen Master Magu was steep and formidable, he abandoned his studies of the written word and went specifically to seek instruction. Upon seeing him, Magu immediately—
Knowing him to be such a man, he went straight to the vegetable garden. A true spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) is a great cause and condition;
moreover, they do not merely provide you with worldly comforts. What is to be done? How is it to be done? It simply requires a person who can enter where there is no place to enter.
When he came for the second audience, Magu went straight into the abbot’s quarters and shut the door. Liang-sui suddenly attained great enlightenment;
he had passed directly through the realm of death. He then offered up his confession of death, saying: "Master, do not deceive Liang-sui.
Had I not come to see you, Master, I would have been nearly cheated out of my life by twelve volumes of sutras and treatises. From before...
The attachment to the literal study of sutras and treatises was a sickness that instantly dissolved and crumbled away.
Upon returning to his lecture hall, he said to the assembly, "What you all know, Liang-sui knows entirely; what Liang-sui knows, you all do not know."

If one does not turn the light back upon itself to reflect, how could this exist? Therefore, in the Gate of the Patriarchs (Zongmen), it makes no distinction between monk and layperson, noble and lowly;

all may turn toward it. Thus, from former times, great scholars such as Prime Minister Li Ao, Prime Minister Pei Xiu, Imperial Secretary Dongpo Su Shi, Lord Han Yu, Zhang Wujin, and Yang Woei—these high-ranking officials of the imperial court—[have all followed this path].
In his youth, he studied the classics and passed the civil service examinations; having attained the highest rank and served as an official, he reached the ultimate limits of Confucianism.

Thus, he was one who mastered both antiquity and the present, whose fame soared and flourished. He was thoroughly proficient in both Buddhism and Daoism, yet he also knew that these were not the ultimate truth.

Urgently turn your head and shift your perspective to seek out a true teacher (*kishi*). Among those who are often clever and sharp-witted, it is difficult for those who are half-believing and half-doubting to gain entry.
As for those who are truly clever and sharp-witted, provided they do not retreat, if they exert themselves with a mind and body as firm as iron or stone, realization is extremely easy to attain.
Have you not seen how Prime Minister Yu Ti studied under Master Ziyu of Yaoshan?

"Venerable elders, I have read through all the common teachings of both Confucianism and Buddhism without exception; I shall simply take the passages that I find doubtful to serve as the basis for my questions.
One day, he suddenly asked: "What is it like when black winds blow their ship and cast it adrift into the realm of rākṣasa demons?
The Ancient Sage immediately pointed directly at the crown of his head and struck him a painful blow, replying: "..."
"Yuti, you hired laborer, what are you talking about? Yuti, the Excellency, had a look of rage on his face.
The Ancient Sage pointed and said, "This is precisely what it means for a black wind to blow one's ship and cast it adrift into the realm of the rākṣasa demons.
Upon these words, Yuti suddenly attained awakening. One must believe that the Buddha-dharma has no partiality; only those of great capacity can withstand it.
This harsh and biting method is worlds apart from those who are hesitant, wavering, and full of doubt; it is as different as heaven and earth. Thus, an ancient worthy said:
"When practicing Chan, practice until there is no more practicing; practice until there is no more practicing, and only then will you reach the ultimate.
Furthermore, another elder said: "When practicing Chan, practice until there is no more practicing; yet even when there is no more practicing, you have not yet reached the ultimate."
It is just like pressing a gourd down into the water; how can one grasp it? Ultimately, what is it? With one punch, he topples Yellow Crane Tower;
with one kick, he overturns Yingwu Isle. When there is spirit, he adds to that spirit;
where there is no elegance, he is nonetheless elegant. Again, Master Zanyuan of Jiangshan was once asked by Lord Jing (Wang Anshi) and Prince Shu (Wang Shen): [The story continues...]

The questioner asked, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? Jiangshan did not answer. After the Prince of Shu had questioned him for a long time, Jiangshan, having no other choice, said to him:
"Your Majesty possesses a resolute and grand nature, and your worldly karmic conditions are profound. With such a resolute and grand nature..."
"He will surely be able to shoulder the heavy burden of the world on his own person. Yet, if his employment or dismissal cannot be guaranteed, his mind will not be at peace.
With a mind that is not at peace, how can one achieve 'ten thousand years in a single thought'? The Master commented, "How great was Chan Master Dazhan!"
Although he wore straw sandals, he walked a thousand or ten thousand times within the belly of King Shu;
yet he did not realize that this "stern and great spirit" (*gang-da zhi qi*) is precisely the fundamental root of this Way and the source of the Buddha-dharma.

Originally, he intended to deceive people face-to-face, but little did he know that it would instead turn into deceiving himself. At that time, had King Shu peeled back his own skin, where could he have found Jiangshan?
"Even so, it is easy to see King Shu, but difficult to see Mount Jiangshan. Now tell me, where does the crux lie?
Do you all understand? [He strikes the meditation seat once with his whisk.
'Bo Ya and Ziqi were no ordinary acquaintances. He then descended from the seat.
