Recorded Sayings of Wuan Heshang, Volume Two:
Record of the Dharma-Abiding at Jianchang Xingguo Chan Monastery on Mount Jufu.
Compiled by the Attendants Dōshō, Kyōyū, and Zenryō.
Ascending the Seat to Offer Congratulations to the Emperor: Sitting upon the seat, he lowers his hook. Having emerged from the oil vat, he enters the soy sauce vat;
his entire body is a mouth—how can he speak? His old fists still possess some strength. He risks his life to provide this mechanism as a guiding compass. Is there anyone? Is there?
"Mo. A monk stepped forward and asked, "The spring light stretches to the horizon, reflecting upon the waters; the sedge on the banks and the grass on the marshes are lush and green.

Seizing this moment, we wish to respond to your earnest invitation, fully unfolding the breeze of compassion to revitalize the ancestral wind. As a student who has come before you, I pray to hear the primary truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
The Master said, "The bright sun hangs in the sky; the clear breeze pervades the earth. The monk pressed further, "When all Buddhas appear in the world..."

[The Emperor asked: "Golden lotuses have sprouted from the earth. As you, the Venerable Master, have come to preside over this mountain, what auspicious omens have there been? The Master replied: "Splitting open Mount Hua, its beauty reaches the heavens;

releasing the Yellow River, its current flows clear. [The Emperor] further asked: "Not only does the establishment of Chang [Temple] increase the auspicious vapors, but the eight directions are stirred with joyful celebration.
The Master replied: "Spring travels through the myriad nations; the moon is reflected in a thousand rivers. [The Emperor] further asked: "The Great Tang..."

"The country is the land of Japan; our school’s style flourishes even more, with no difference whatsoever. "How is the Buddha-dharma of the Great Tang? The Master said, "One blow, one trace of a welt.
[The monk] further asked, "How is the Buddha-dharma of the land of Japan? The Master said, "One slap, one palmful of blood.

[The monk] further asked, "If it is thus, then when one point is penetrated, a thousand points and ten thousand points are all penetrated at once. The Master said: *Note: The final response from the Master is left as in the source text, as it is an open-ended, non-verbal cue typical of this genre.*
"Only you alone do not yet know the nature of pain and pleasure.

The monk asked, "As for the Great Donor, Duke of the State, who specifically requested the Master to ascend the hall and expound the Dharma, the Master declined several times with formal letters and further offered fifteen verses to plead his refusal.
Why, in the end, was he unable to decline? The Master said, "Had I known the affairs of today earlier, I would have regretted it."
[The Master] said, "You were not careful at the beginning. The student said, "It can be said that the Way of Buddha after Buddha is the same, for their compassionate vows are profound;

they extensively open the way to benefit and rescue the common people. The Master said, "Better that such good things had never happened. The student said, "On this day, the Duke of the Palace has personally arrived to listen respectfully to the essentials of the Dharma.
Ultimately, how will you instruct him? The Master said, "The pavilion by the water is the first to catch the moon; the flower facing the sun..."
"The trees meet spring early. The student said, "If that is so, then it is like adding thousands upon thousands of layers of flowers atop brocade.

The Master said, "This single phrase is indeed quite similar. He then said, "Before the Buddhas appeared in the world and before the Patriarchs came from the West, everyone’s true wisdom was serene and still;
what a peaceful and tranquil world it was! Without cause, the seeds of the barbarians sprouted, and thus poison was seen."
Evil spreads; on level ground, spears and halberds clash. Without wind, waves arise, leading inevitably to the partitioning of borders and the shifting of east to fill the west.
Thorns pierce the heavens, and creeping vines cover the earth. And yet, even so—how can one transmit the message before the world was established and before the Buddhas and Patriarchs had appeared?
After a long silence, he said: "The whale swallows the ocean until it is exhausted, revealing the coral reef."
Huzhi again raised the case of Master Linji. When Attendant Wang visited him, they went together into the Sangha Hall.
The Attendant asked, "Do the monks in this hall practice seated meditation? Linji said, "They do not practice seated meditation.

The Attendant asked, "Then do they study the scriptures? Linji said, "They do not study the scriptures. The Attendant said, "If they neither practice seated meditation nor study the scriptures, what exactly are they doing?"
"What is it? Linji said, "I simply want to cause everyone to become a Buddha or a Patriarch. Wang said, "Though gold dust is precious, when it falls into the eye, it becomes a cataract.
Linji said, "I thought you were just an ordinary fellow. The Master [Zhaozhou] commented: "Old man Linji’s breath swallowed the entire universe;
he wanted nothing more than to test and break through everyone. Yet he was casually broken through by Attendant Wang. Do you all understand?"
Do you understand? Listen now to this commentary: one push followed by another, one kick followed by another punch—throughout past and present, there has never been a lapse;
it is clearly right before one’s eyes.
That evening, during the informal discourse (*xiaochan*), a monk came forward and asked: "Empty-handed, one grasps a hoe; walking, one rides a water buffalo.

A person passes over the bridge, yet the bridge flows while the water does not flow. What is the meaning of this? The Master said: "A vajra strikes, and the iron mountain crumbles. The monk pressed further:
"What is 'empty-handed, one grasps a hoe'? The Master said: "Even the thousand sages find it difficult to grasp. The monk pressed further.
[The student] asked, "What is it like to walk while riding a water buffalo? The Master said, "If you look at it, you will go blind.
[The student] further asked, "When a person passes over a bridge, the bridge flows but the water does not flow; what about that? The Master said, "That is still somewhat close."
It is said: "There is a phrase and there is no phrase, like a vine leaning against a tree; when the tree falls, the vine withers. To what place do the phrases return?

One must know that verbal expression cannot reach it and description can hardly capture it. In Muzhou Daowu’s smile lies a blade, which has led to his being hailed as a preeminent master throughout the monastic communities.
Thus it is, thus it is. Great difficulty, great difficulty! As soon as there is a single strand of thread, there are a hundred strands.
A lion’s single drop of milk scatters a hundred jars of donkey’s milk. And yet, even so, it only adds to the ever-fresh laughter of Guishan.
Again, Master Luyuan addressed the assembly, saying: "The very intent of the one who came from the West is indeed difficult to express.
At that time, a monk stepped forward. Luyuan struck him across the back and said: "What kind of time is this now for you to show your head?"
He then returned to the abbot’s quarters. The Master commented: "The orthodox command was not carried out; he twisted the crooked to make it straight.
Had this monk known the nature of pain and itch, the milk source would not have returned to the abbot’s quarters."
Ascending the hall, he said: "Having cast off the thousand-pound burden, one should simply seek tranquility wherever one is.

Yet, in my old age, I have not yet escaped the karmic debts; I have fallen once more into the single barrier of Kenjō-ji. My voice is still indistinct and responding to others remains difficult. For both speaker and listener, it is difficult beyond measure.
Relying solely on this single white staff, whether you come from the south or the north, I shall give each of you a severe blow. Suddenly, he struck."
Put on one or half a piece of utterly liberated [attire], and let it be known that it is not at all within the realm of speech or non-speech.
The Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the teachings are all but pointing to emptiness and speaking of emptiness—scattering earth and scattering sand. Ultimately, how is it?
Plucking willow blossoms, plucking willow blossoms.

The Buddha ascends the hall on his birthday. As soon as he was born from the right side, he immediately let loose his blind ignorance, pointing at heaven and pointing at earth, walking with independent stride in every direction.
Yunmen would have beaten him to death; Jianchang assisted in digging the pit. Let this evil seed be taught never to sprout again. Nevertheless—
This is also like "drawing the bow after the thief has fled.
Entering the retreat, I ascend the hall: yesterday was sunny, today it rains; spring and summer pass one another in their proper sequence.

It is just like a monk of the forest who never oversteps the rules. For three months of *an-guo* (summer retreat), one takes up the period according to the fixed schedule. In the West, they use wax...
"Human ice. Yunfeng uses an iron ball; Jianchang likewise has a single path of life: when hungry, eat; when thirsty, drink; when idle, sit;
when exhausted, sleep. Taking this as your basis, everyone should simply investigate in this manner;
you will certainly not be deceived.

Small-scale *sǎn* (private instruction) upon the conclusion of the summer retreat: "The Buddha expounds the Dharma with a single sound, yet sentient beings each attain understanding according to their kind.
I venture to ask the assembly: what, then, is this Dharma expounded by that single sound? Is it that heaven is heaven and earth is earth?
"Are the mountains the mountains and the waters the waters? Or are they the spring growth and summer flourishing, the autumn harvest and winter storage?
To theorize in such a manner is much like poking through fire to seek a bubble. Now tell me, what is that single sound? [The Master] strikes the meditation seat with his whisk and says:
"Once this single sound is proclaimed, it pervades the entire universe and the great earth, reaching all who are holy or ordinary, their emotions and..."
"Insentient beings, upon hearing this Dharma-sound, all attain awakening and understanding. Nevertheless, although this is so, only the whisk does not enter this protective community.
Why? Have you not heard it said: 'This mountain monk does not calculate the cyclical sexagenary cycle; when a single leaf falls, one knows the autumn of the world'?
[The Master] then strikes once more."
Ascending the hall, he said: "Unbinding the mouth of the cloth bag, one attains freedom in every direction. In going, there is no restraint;
in departing, one travels to the southern and northern regions. One herds the water-buffalo of Mt. Mui; even where there is no elegance, there is elegance."
Xie, the two Librarians, ascended the hall. Holding up his staff, he called to the assembly, saying: "The Great Canon and the Lesser Canon all flow forth from this very place.
If you can discern where they fall, the business of a lifetime of study is finished. If not yet so, [do not delay]."
Now listen to this staff as it points them out from the beginning. It strikes once to the left and says: "This is the teaching of existence.
It strikes once to the right and says: "This is the teaching of emptiness. It strikes once in the middle and says:
"This is the Middle Way Mahāyāna teaching. These three sections are distinct; should one wish to explain this sutra, the subsequent text is long, and it is entrusted to the future.
On that day, [the Master] struck the wooden fish once more.
The Duke proceeded to his own temple to perform a ritual for the fulfillment of vows and prayers. He formally requested a general discourse (which includes questions and answers, here not recorded).
It is said: "A great person possesses great vision; with great wisdom, they attain great function. Containing the six realms within their breast, they grasp the heavens and earth in their hands.
Seated upon the emerald oil-silk couch, they don the armor of patience, hold the arrow of firmness, and wield the bow of wisdom.

They take the entire great chiliocosm as a single battlefield and point to the ten billion Mount Sumerus as a single target for archery. Shooting a hundred times, they hit the mark a hundred times; they release both [arrows] at once."
Gathering both [powers], he sweeps away millions of malevolent demons and utterly eradicates the evil factions of Pūtanā. Thus, one beholds a time of clarity and the Way’s prosperity;

the seas are calm and the rivers clear. The eight directions submit to benevolence, and the myriad states present their tribute. He halts his reins in self-delight, sitting in firm tranquility without anxiety.
One might say that I have attained mastery over the Dharma within the Dharma King. At such a moment, tell me: where does the merit reside?
After a long silence, he said: "Without raising a single blade, the demons' hearts were shattered; they raised their banners of surrender upon hearing the wind."
It is further said: "The Buddha taught all dharmas in order to deliver all minds. If there were no minds, what use would there be for all dharmas?
This is because all sentient beings, from time immemorial, have lacked wisdom and harbored perverse attachments, thereby giving rise to delusions and creating karma.
Wandering through the five realms of saṃsāra, when a Tathāgata appears in the world, he teaches the sublime principle of the Middle Way according to what is appropriate for beings,

enabling all sentient beings to thoroughly understand all phenomena, to distance themselves from doubt and attachment, to give rise to the practice of the Middle Way, and to each cultivate it to fulfillment so as to attain the three types of enlightenment.

The realization of the bliss of nirvana is entirely the work of the mind. An ancient worthy said: "This very mind, mind, mind is the Buddha; it is the most wondrous entity in the worlds of the ten directions.
Its marvelous functions, manifesting freely, are truly pitiable in their excellence; nothing else compares to the reality of the mind.
Observing the five precepts leads to birth in the human realm, and practicing the ten wholesome deeds leads to birth in the heavenly realms—all these are produced by the mind. As for renunciation...
To enter the outflow-free from the outflowing, and to abandon the conditioned to enter the unconditioned—all this is wrought by the mind.
Indeed, because the cultivation of good and evil differs, the Buddhas appear in the world;

observing the faculties [of beings], they provide teachings suited to them, expounding the Dharma-gates of the Three Vehicles, and even manifesting various bodies according to each respective class of being to preach the Dharma for them. This Dharma is but a single Dharma, for...
Possessing all these states of mind, he teaches all dharmas according to the capacities of beings.

Although he teaches in accordance with their faculties, within the great assembly of devas and humans, there are those who realize the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and those who attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Yet, there are also those within the assembly who are like the deaf or the blind, unable to understand. This is because realization and awakening vary in depth.
There are degrees of excellence in attaining the Way. Sometimes it is taught cryptically and then explained openly; sometimes it speaks of emptiness and then reveals reality;

sometimes it points directly to the principle of the special transmission outside the teachings. All of this is intended solely for all people to clarify their own minds, perceive their own nature, and realize this Dharma.
This Dharma is neither existent nor non-existent; it is neither existence-and-non-existence nor the absence of both. If you say the Way does not reside in words...
As for the teachings of this one lifetime, where can they be situated? If you say they reside in the place of exposition, then how is this Dharma expounded?
One must have possessed spiritual bone from former lives and possess firm roots of faith to have the capacity to enter into it.

Therefore, the Great Dānapati, having long ago mounted the power of his vows, has deeply believed in the Buddha-Dharma with earnest devotion and has transcribed the entire Tripitaka, reading, examining, and reciting it.

He maintained this, yet knew it was not the ultimate. By this power, he investigated the meaning of the "separate transmission outside the teachings," striving tirelessly without ceasing, never forgetting it even while eating or resting, taking full realization as his goal.
Thus, one knows him to be a Bodhisattva of great capacity and great power who has returned for a second time.
Only then can one act in this manner. Furthermore, he was able to establish a great monastery as the foremost *āyatana* in the kingdom, providing extensive peace for many followers.

He caused each of them to understand the regulations and protocols of a great monastic grove (*saṃghārāma*), each to investigate the great matter of their own person, and each to know the profound and vast purport of the "separate transmission outside the teachings," which can continue the Buddha’s life of wisdom and enable one to transcend birth.
Dying on this shore, one reaches the other shore of Bodhi and Nirvana, extensively delivering sentient beings so that all may attain Buddhahood.
One must constantly cultivate this mind, making it ever firmer and more enduring. Can one truly act in such a way? This old monk was born and raised in the land of Shu;

I have wandered the rivers and lakes seeking the Way for many years. Recently, due to the principle of not forgetting old ties among Dharma relatives, I repeatedly received invitations, yet I have persistently declined them.
I arrived once more for that reason. Having settled my temple affairs, I took advantage of a favorable opportunity to cross the desert to observe the splendor of the state.

I was first received by the Duke of the State (Guogong), who granted me a special audience; upon seeing me, he treated me as an old friend. Although we could not yet communicate through speech, in all matters of movement and stillness, coming and going, speaking and silence, or responding to one another, our hearts and eyes shone upon each other.
It was evident from this alone that it was because I am a kinsman of the Way that such a thing occurred.
Thus it is. One immediately beholds the old man Gautama, who throughout more than three hundred and sixty assemblies, has proclaimed this Dharma—whether among humans or in the heavens.
Speaker and listener, heart and heart, knew one another; eye and eye, illuminated one another.
This is no different from what is being spoken and heard today. Therefore it is said: "All kalpas of the past are placed within the present and the future. Unfolding...
Taking the present eon and placing it back into the past eon, one clearly penetrates until the boundaries of the past and future are severed. The three great kalpas are empty;

one perceives that from the beginningless aeons down to the present, there is not even a hair’s breadth of discrepancy. Within the ordinary mind and the measure of the sage, one seeks even a hair’s breadth and finds nothing at all.
This is what is meant by: "In a single thought-moment, universally contemplate immeasurable kalpas; there is no going, no coming, and no abiding. It is like...
This is the thorough knowledge of the three periods of time; transcending all expedient means, one accomplishes the Ten Powers.

When a student of the Way penetrates to the depths here, seeing through the local scenery of their own original ground and their fundamental face with vivid clarity, they will finally know that every sentence and every word of the teachings given throughout a single lifetime does not speak of anything else, and is no different from the principle of the separate transmission outside the teachings.

They are distinct. Whether one attains realization through the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the teachings, or attains realization through the intent of the separate transmission outside the teachings, both are paths that lead home.
Realization attained within the teachings is ultimately circuitous; realization attained outside the teachings is direct and unimpeded.
Only this single direct path can surely lead one home; it surely leads to the Great [Awakening].
This is the field of great rest; until the end of the future, one shall attain great mastery. Why?

Because by transcending the mind, intellect, and consciousness (*citta-manovijñāna*), and departing from the paths of both the holy and the ordinary, one may then be called "direct. Only those of great capacity and great power are fit for such refinement.
Impermanence is swift; do not treat it with indifference. As the ancient masters said: "Exert yourself; you must bring this life to completion."

Stop! Do not let yourself suffer further calamities for eternal kalpas. It is certain that a human body is difficult to obtain, a favorable time is difficult to encounter, a spiritual friend is difficult to meet, and the True Dharma is difficult to hear.

Now that you have obtained a human body, with the *kāṣāya* robe upon your person—a favorable time having been encountered, a spiritual friend having been met, and the True Dharma having been heard—if you utterly fail to take this as a matter of urgency, it is surely because you have never planted the seeds of *prajñā*.

Regarding the seed: hearing seems like not hearing; seeing seems like not seeing; encountering seems like not encountering. Many miss their opportunity because they harbor this "all-encompassing mind.
It is for this reason that the Buddha taught all dharmas.

From spring through summer into autumn, I have followed your instructions to establish a ritual site for prayer for the sake of the nation and the people, leading [the assembly] three times daily—at dawn, noon, and dusk.
The great assembly has diligently cultivated, perused, recited, and upheld [this teaching], single-mindedly praying for abundant harvests and universal peace.
Now that these earnest prayers have indeed been fulfilled, I shall ascend the seat this day to deliver a general discourse for the assembly.

In doing so, I shall speak this Dharma with this very mind, moving the Buddhas, the dragons, and the devas to witness this sincere prayer. This is the most auspicious among all auspicious things, and the most sublime among all sublime things. It is thus...

This is the spiritual efficacy of this mind and these dharmas. Among those brothers who strive for the Way within the assembly, whether they have attained realization within the teachings or outside the teachings, many are like the wind passing through trees; it is evident that this is no small matter.
The decline of the Buddha-dharma has never been more severe than it is today.

Wherever this old monk has stayed in monasteries, he has often seen brothers among the assembly who strive for the Way with such earnestness and urgency that they do not spare a moment, day or night, taking the full realization of the Great Matter as their goal.
Among them, there have occasionally been one or two who have emerged to propagate and uphold the Great Dharma, many of whom continue to transcend the boundaries of past and present. If...
This path of mindfulness is not firm; one’s strength is not great. In the end, it will be difficult to hope for the Great Dharma.
Have you not seen what Zhaozhou said? "Everyone is driven by the twelve periods of the day, but I alone am able to drive the twelve periods.
Now tell me, where did he go wrong? If you all were truly diligent and earnest, you would simply take this very self—
This matter of life and death is a great affair. Day and night, three times each, you must confront it face-to-face, refusing to let go for even a single moment.
Only then will you clearly attain the twelve hours of the day. If you merely wait for today or tomorrow to examine this "Zhang San" or that "Li Si," you will never find it.
To hear someone say something is good and immediately agree it is good, or to hear someone say it is not good and further declare it is not good—this is called "the dwarf watching the play.
One merely follows others up and down; as for oneself, one remains in total darkness. In vain, one wastes time, unaware that old age and sickness are approaching.
When birth and death arrive, with what will you resist them? There is no doubt that you will end up in the womb of a donkey or the belly of a horse.
This is because one has, in vain, consumed the faithful offerings of donors and unworthily received the sustenance of humans and devas.
One abandons one's own spiritual practice and speaks only of the faults and evils of others; if others have no faults or evils, one fabricates and falsely asserts them.
To do so is to increase one's own [karmic burden]. How can one escape the three miserable realms and the hells? This is the definitive meaning, in accord with the scriptures and teachings.
What has been spoken is entirely consistent; it is certainly not a word of deception or jest.

Whether you believe it or not, the old monk has made a thousand errors and ten thousand mistakes. Having recently arrived here from beyond the desert, my decrepit physical form has yet to master the local dialect.
Yet, unable to refuse the imperial command, I have exerted myself to sustain the office of abbot, ascending the hall, entering the room, and delivering public sermons for the assembly.
Although he had never lacked for anything, when lowering his hands [in a gesture of humility], he sighed to himself that he had wasted his spirit.

Generally speaking, those who have left the household life and place themselves within the monastic community—donning the Buddha’s *kāṣāya*, dwelling in the Buddha’s house, and eating the Buddha’s food—must surely uphold the Buddha’s precepts.
To cultivate the Buddha’s practice, propagate the Buddha’s Dharma, and continue the Buddha’s life of wisdom;

or to come forth to manage affairs and assist the monastic community—this must be done from beginning to end, with complete excellence and perfection, so as to establish the enduring precedents of the monastery. Only by thus accomplishing this can one truly accomplish oneself;
only then is one called a "Chan practitioner" (chanhezi) and may one be termed a disciple of the Buddha. Otherwise, for what reason could one attain greatness?
When one has performed a thousand tasks, they must all be brought to completion;

when the thirtieth day of the twelfth month arrives, it is as if not a single basketful of earth has been added to the field of the monastic robes, and one falls into the Iron Ring Mountains amidst the suffering of a hundred punishments. Of whom is this the fault? It is surely because their aspiration for the Way was not firm and their strength was not great;
such are the distinctions that arise. This is what is meant by the decline of the Buddha-dharma being no more severe than it is today. If...
I speak of this mind and these dharmas until the end of the future, without exhaustion.

May all those gathered here who hear and listen receive the prediction of enlightenment under the Dragon Flower Tree. I offer this verse to fulfill my vow of the heart, presenting it to the great assembly:

"Applying this mind for the sake of the nation and the people, The fruit accords with earnest prayers, obtaining abundance and prosperity. When times are clear and the Way is tranquil, [all shall be] sealed [in peace]."
The borders are vast and wide; the entire nation rejoices, celebrating peace. Ascending the hall, he said:
"When a single mote of dust enters right concentration (*samādhi*), all motes arise in *samādhi*. When all motes enter right concentration, a single mote arises in *samādhi*.
As for *samādhi* and right reception (*samyak-samāpatti*), they are washed within the mud of the earth. Heh! In broad daylight, one clearly sees ghosts with one's own eyes."
"It is not non-being, nor is it being; it is not right, nor is it wrong. Under the Jiazi and Yichou stems, there is the Gold in the Sea;
under the Bingwu and Dingwei stems, there is the Water of the Heavenly River. If you people do not understand, listen as this staff points directly at you.
(He strikes once and says: "Today is the first day of the ninth month; tomorrow is the second. (He strikes again.)
The assembly ascended to the Hall. It was said: "This is the Festival of Opening the Furnace; how can it be described? There is no talk of guest or host; frost and snow are held in the mouth.
Having encountered one who understands, I shall briefly pick up the theme for you all. You must by no means provoke this recklessly; remain silent and guard it.
Suddenly, when a bean pops in cold ashes, only then will you know that the seeds of the civil and military fires are difficult to extinguish."
The news of the passing of his two dharma brothers, Bieshan and Duanjiao, arrived. He ascended the hall and said:
"The white-fanged beast of the Southern Mountain has struck down the Peak of Taibai, causing West Lake to dry up to its very depths and the angry waves of the Eastern Sea to overturn the void.
Guifeng of Anhan claps his hands; the Venerable of Tiantai beats his breast in haste. In the land of Japan they beat the drum; in the land of Great Tang..."
He strikes the bell. Why? "Brothers, add ten characters. Who can fathom this meaning? He slaps his knee once and lets out a sigh.
He descends from the seat.

The Dharma-brother from Tōfuku-ji ascends the hall. Having drunk together from the dragon spring and sat together at the teacher’s seat, we polished one another through mutual refinement and benefited each other through mutual nourishment.
Now that we have parted ways, heading east and west, each shall uphold the ancestral command. You have crossed the desert to come here and offer yourself; I have surrendered my heart and soul to you.

As we take our leave, exactly one circuit of a thousand li has passed. May you look down upon us with your radiant influence; let the entire assembly once again receive your compassionate light, no different from stirring the embers.
The clouds see the sun. Whether moving upward or downward, they all lean against one side of the wall.
Why is this? I recall the house of the Lingxiao poison; not even a single drop of water ever touched it. A-he-he! Do you understand?
The green mountains do not lock the soaring momentum; the vast blue sea surely knows its lofty origin.

Ascending the hall, he said: "I came to this land originally to transmit the Dharma and save deluded beings. One flower opens into five petals; the fruiting occurs naturally. He then held up his staff and said:
"The Old Barbarian (Bodhidharma) received the prophetic record from Prajñātāra. He traveled ten thousand *li* with great toil, crossing the sea to arrive here.
He roamed through Liang and passed through Wei, sitting in cold seclusion for nine years. Even until he divided the skin and the marrow, one would have thought there was much more to it."
He possessed little of the extraordinary; yet, when it came to the single verse of the transmission of the Dharma, his deficiencies were seen to be no small matter.
Although Kenchō was a direct descendant in the orthodox lineage, he never once set foot upon his territory. Now, as the anniversary of his death approaches, [I offer this].

On account of the vegetarian feast and celebratory praise, there is also one verse which I shall present to the great assembly: I have come to this land from of old, With no dharma to transmit to others.
Those who become snakes enter the grass; Those who become dragons ascend to heaven.
The two novice monks who serve as the primary fundraisers for Wannian Temple on Mount Tiantai ascend to the hall.
A person has come from Mount Tiantai and brought news from Xichuan, reporting that the Wannian Pine grows atop the Stone Bridge. Fenggan was not right to be so talkative.
For the sake of Lei, Shi-de, Han-shan, and others, he exerted himself regardless of his own person, traveling far south and north until he rushed directly to the dragon palace in the Eastern Sea.
There he sought out the bright pearl beneath the chin of the azure dragon, embraced it and returned, bringing vast benefit.

Not only did it illuminate the ten voids and its radiance swallow the myriad phenomena, but it even caused the great ocean to transform into mulberry fields. This is the Great Compassion of the Thousand Hands.
Its radiance was further enhanced. Five hundred great beings were startled into awakening;

each arose from their meditative concentration, split open the Yeungpyeong Peak, and sucked dry the waters of the Broken Bridge. Joining their palms, they praised him, saying: "Excellent, excellent! Rare, rare indeed!
This is the eternal glory of the Great Tang and Japan, able to transcend all bounds. Nevertheless, [the Master] struck them with his staff.
Regarding the "One Perfect Circle" (yī yuánxiàng), he asked: "Do you all still know the origin of this great jewel? He struck the ground once and said:
"If it were easily obtained, one would simply regard it as something trivial. He then threw down his staff and descended from the seat.
Upon receiving the news of Xiyuan’s passing, he ascended the hall and said: "Recently, a messenger arrived from afar to convey word that these past years have been relatively peaceful.
Yet, only Taibai and Ruyuan Gong have shattered the void into fragments.
This startles the Stone Woman atop Mount Dapeng in Western Sichuan until her tears fall in pairs, and draws forth the Wooden Man in Mount Jufu in Fusang to sigh in vain."
[He] paused. "Tell me, why is it so? After a long silence, he said: "We drink together from the same dragon-pool of meaningless water;
our bond of righteousness is as heavy as glue and lacquer. He struck his knee and said: "A snapped string—how can it be mended with phoenix-glue?"
Winter Solstice Small Sermon: The Perfect Circle is identical to the Great Void; it is neither deficient nor redundant. It is only because of grasping and rejecting that one falls short.
Have you not heard it said: "When I press my finger, the Sea-Seal emits light"? Here, as soon as the eye sees, the ghost departs; this is no mere matter of error.

Should you momentarily raise your mind, you will immediately see the afflictions of the mundane world arise first. You must know that when the six dark forces (*ṣaḍ-tamāṃsi*) are completely stripped away, [the light of wisdom shines forth].
Yet there is no trace of its being stripped away; the single Yang reappears, yet there is no mark of its reappearing.
Since there are no traces, it is utterly beyond reception or apprehension. An iron tree blossoms, its fragrance overwhelming the nose.
Again, he cited Master Yunmen’s ascent of the hall. A monk asked, “I ask the Master to answer my question. Yunmen called out, “The assembly! The assembly raised their heads;
Yunmen immediately descended from his seat. The Master commented: “Yunmen answering the question in such a manner has already let his tongue trail on the ground.
Nevertheless, even if one were to realize it before the words were uttered, that too would already be unfit for serious discussion. Why?”
Furthermore, he covered it over for those to come. Then, raising his voice, he called to the assembly; the assembly looked up. He said again, "As expected," and then descended from the seat.

On the occasion of the Winter Solstice, he ascended the hall and said: "The winter solstice and the one hundred and fifth day of the cold food festival—within these lies a single turn of plain, substantial words. [He then] showed his missing tooth.
The Old Barbarian did not lift it all; he deceived that man standing in the snow, who was reckless and crude. Do you all wish to know? After a long silence, he said:
"A cat is especially adept at catching mice."
Ascending the hall: On the eighth night of the twelfth month, one sees ghosts with one's own eyes and then opens a wide mouth to discourse on principle.
If such a person passes before the gate of a patch-robed monk, there is no doubt they will receive a thorough beating with a rotten mallet. Is there anyone here who would lend a hand or lend a kick?
Speaking in the Japanese dialect: *Wasuru wa*.

At Saemyeongsa Temple, His Majesty responded to a dream by visiting his home temple and ordering the monks to recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* ten thousand scrolls to pray for the peace and stability of the realm.
He requested that the ceremony be concluded with the Master ascending the seat. (The questions and answers are not recorded. The Master then said: "All conditioned phenomena..."
"Like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, and a shadow; like dew and also like lightning—thus should one contemplate. [The Master] suddenly called to the assembly, saying:
"One who contemplates in this way is said to have right contemplation; if one contemplates otherwise, it is called wrong contemplation.

If this were within the gate of proclaiming the teachings, it would be enough to deceive gods and mock ghosts; but within the gate of the patch-robed monks, it is much like coming out of Caozhou while in Zhengzhou.

[This is] the Gate. Although the old man Gautama proclaimed [this truth] from within the midst of non-existence during the assembly on Prajñāpāramitā, how could it be said that in the final five hundred years, one is bound like a blind donkey and lacks the capacity for freedom?

Have you not seen how the Ge-lao, for no reason, upon hearing the recitation of "one should give rise to the mind by dwelling nowhere," immediately mistook the donkey’s saddle-bridge for his father’s chin, thereby bringing about [his own] entanglement.
Furthermore, regarding Zhou Jingang, who burned a volume of commentaries and sub-commentaries and then dared to brandish his staff and strike recklessly—this was truly groundless.

Little did he know that within the imperial treasury there is no such blade. One must understand that the Buddhas of the three periods speak of dreams, and the patriarchs of successive generations speak of dreams.
When one person transmits a falsehood, ten thousand people transmit it as truth; thus it has filled the lands of India and Tang China. Do not...

He was able to suppress it, yet [the other] remained unaware and ignorant. It subsequently spread to Japan, where at the temple of Saimei-ji, under the bright sun and clear sky, he spoke of dreams with eyes wide open, as if he had personally seen and heard them on Vulture Peak; there was no difference and no distinction.
Jōchō possessed spirit but lacked the source of authority, and thus failed to recognize right from wrong. Therefore, I confronted him before the assembly in the Daikyū-den and exposed his deception.
In a world of purity and peace, one must strictly avoid false rumors. Let us simply bring about universal tranquility, where weapons are laid aside and war ceases;
where the state is secure and the people are at ease; where harvests are bountiful and seasons are prosperous. When hungry, eat; when thirsty, drink; when idle, sit; when weary, sleep.

Be without intention regarding affairs, and be without affairs regarding intention. Without desire and without dependence—how joyful and liberating this is! Yet, even though it is thus, when you scoop up water...
The moon is in his hand; playing with the fragrance of flowers, they fill his robes. Again, he raises the question of Śāriputra to Subhūti:
"Is the teaching of the six *pāramitās* within a dream the same as or different from that of the waking state? Subhūti replied, "This meaning is profound and subtle;
I am unable to explain it. In this assembly there is the Great Being Maitreya; go to him and ask. [The Master] then remarked: "Śāriputra opened [the way]."
The Eye speaks of dreams; Subhūti utters words while asleep. Jianchang suppressed his indignation and resentment all at once.
Thereupon he composed a verse and presented it to the assembly: "In a dream, one expounds the Six Pāramitās; Upon waking, one asks another about their similarities and differences.
Today, the most luminous re-explanation is given; Not a single word contains any ambiguity. A-he-he! Do you understand?"
"Ema! How wonderful it is that this is a day of peace and no affairs; yet, even so, I do not permit the raising of arms. (He lets out a shout.

On the anniversary of the passing of Fojian of Jingshan, he offered incense, saying: "On the eighteenth day of the third month every year, I remember his grievance with such intensity that it pierces to the very marrow of my bones."
Gazing toward the Azure Clouds from Mount Jufu, ten thousand layers of mountains and seas spread out in vast waves of mist.
In vain, one burns a stick of *tūlasi* wood: Oṃ (protracted), *pèn pèn fā fā*.
Chuliao inscribed these verses on the *Amitābha Sūtra* and sent them to the hall of Zuiming Temple:
"I possess a great scripture, Its measure equal to the three thousandfold world-system. I personally entrust it to the hall of Zuiming, To pray for a longevity as vast as the ocean."
I only wish to obtain this sutra and immediately clarify this mind, so as to know with certainty that the Patriarch Bodhidharma was originally not at Shaolin.

On the sixteenth day of the tenth month in the year of Renxu, at the Most Bright Monastery (Zuiming Si), Zuiming posed a question, saying: "Recently, while practicing seated meditation, I have perceived that..."

"Neither annihilation nor permanence is the bottom. The Master said, "In practicing Chan, one seeks only to see one's nature. If you attain the seeing of your nature, only then will you achieve complete and total resolution.
Zuiming asked, "Please, Master, provide an expedient instruction. The Master said, "There is no second path under heaven, and no dual mind in the sages.
If you recognize the mind of the sage, that is precisely your own original source-nature. Zuiming [responded].

Ming said, "Your disciple, Daochong, has no mind. The Master said, "If you truly have no mind, it extends vertically through the three periods of time and spans horizontally throughout the ten directions.
(Pointing to a candle, he said: "For example, before the wax candle has been poured and formed, it is the natural radiance of the original ground, the original face.
When it is finally poured, lit, and burning, its brilliance is elegant to behold, illuminating the deepest darkness. People—"

People gaze upon it. At the end, when the candle is exhausted and its light reaches its limit, it returns to its original state as before, with no news of change. The Buddha’s appearance in the world to deliver sentient beings is also like this.
Before his appearance in the world, his body of the pure dharma-realm fundamentally has neither arising nor ceasing.

Through the power of his great compassionate vow, he manifests an appearance in the world and the attainment of enlightenment, preaching the three vehicles and the twelve [links of dependent origination] according to the superior, middling, and inferior capacities of beings.

The transmission of the teaching: holding up a flower to show the assembly was intended to cause the great multitude of sages, ordinary people, devas, and humans to clarify their minds and see their nature.
Finally entering *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, it is like a single wax candle—without duality or distinction—circulating through the ages until this very day.
If you see this nature, you will see it directly and immediately. After a long silence, he asked, "Do you see? Zuìmíng replied, "Yes."
"The myriad phenomena of the universe—the mountains, rivers, and the great earth—are non-dual and indistinguishable from one's own self.

The Master said, "The lush green bamboo is entirely True Suchness (Tathatā); the dense yellow flowers are nothing other than Prajñā. At these most lucid words, [the disciple] suddenly attained realization;
his entire body broke into a sweat, and he exclaimed, "For twenty-one years, morning and evening, I have gazed toward this. Now, in a single moment, it is as it was."
Satisfied, he shed several rows of tears and performed nine prostrations. The Master immediately rose, burned incense before the Buddha, and granted him formal authorization (*anujñā*).
He then bestowed upon him his own dharma robe and addressed him, saying: "Sir, you have not easily reached this stage."

"You should protect and uphold [this teaching] well, so that the Dharma may abide for a long time. I personally entrust this dharma-robe to you to symbolize the succession of one lamp from another, thereby continuing the Buddha’s life of wisdom and illuminating the final age, so that it may flourish ever more gloriously for ten thousand generations. Next, he recited for him the verse of the transmission of the Dharma.
I have not spoken even a single word of the Buddha-dharma; you, my son, likewise have no mind and nothing to attain.
Within this state where there is neither speech nor attainment, within this non-mind, Śākyamuni personally beheld Dīpaṃkara Buddha.
After the Abbot of Saimei-ji attained the Way, the Master presented him with five verses on "Assisting the Path":
"When the old monk first arrived, I gave him three blows; He buried his resentment in his breast and harbored this grudge. When his bitter hatred suddenly vanished, he opened the True Eye;
Only then did he know that I did not preach in vain."
Awakening is the same as when one has not yet awakened; Dressing and eating according to the needs of the moment, In rising, sitting, moving, and resting, there is never any difference.
Only then does one believe in the second meaning of the "Plucking of the Flower."
For twenty-one years I endured bitter toil; seeking out the sutras and engaging in debate, I exhausted my spirit.
Suddenly, I grasped my mother-born nose, and laughed aloud at the barbarian monk’s flapping lips.
Governing the state and governing the people are both external matters; preserving the mind and maintaining mindfulness are one's own internal practice.
When the pathways of thought are severed, observe briefly: there is neither Buddha nor Dharma.
On the morning of the sixteenth day of the tenth month in the *Renxu* year, the empty space gave a fist-blow and a kick, leaving no room for evasion.
Once this mass of doubt is casually shattered, even the great earth of gold may as well be consumed.

In a most vivid dream, he encountered a virtuous spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) who instructed him to cultivate Zen with steadfast resolve. Upon awakening, he personally painted [the image] as an offering.
Two years later, when an elderly monk arrived, he went first to pay his respects; indeed, the monk was exactly as he had seen in his dream.
After attaining realization, he presented the portrait he had painted and requested a verse of praise.

Through the refinement of a thousand smeltings and ten thousand forges, the work was brought to maturity. Moved by this, he dreamed of a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) who earnestly exhorted him to apply further effort in practice and cultivation.
Consequently, he attained realization and his mind was fulfilled. He exposed his own ugliness and folly; even the Buddhas and Patriarchs looked up at him, their countenances turning pale with shame.
This old monk shall add yet another layer. (A clap. "Swift as the imperial decree! (Ji ji ru lü ling chi).
In a long letter sent to the Retired Emperor of Saimei-ji, it was stated that the messenger from Saimei-ji reported:
"The Retired Emperor of Saimei-ji has suffered the loss of various goods due to a great wind; the myriad people of the realm are in hardship.
Consequently, Your Majesty’s heart is filled with anxiety and lacks joy. From this, it can be seen that he grieves for others rather than for himself; this is indeed [the mark of a true ruler].
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas employ their minds in this way. Although this old monk is currently ill, I do not worry about myself;

I only worry that the karmic affairs of my disciples have not yet been clarified. This is what is meant by the saying: "In all under heaven there is but one Way, and in the sages there is but one mind."
When the Buddha was in the world, the Gautama clan was about to be overwhelmed by a great calamity of wind and fire. They came in haste to seek refuge with the Buddha to escape it.
The Buddha said, "It cannot be avoided. Why? Because sentient beings have created so much karma that what is induced by collective karma—known as fixed karma—is difficult to escape;
